name: Shea butter

card.summary: A plant fat from African shea nuts used as an emollient; supported mainly by tradition and lab data, with no solo-ingredient appearance trials.
card.note: Refined grades may retain far less of the vitamin and phenolic content than unrefined butter.

quick.overview:
Shea butter is a creamy fat from the nuts of the African shea tree. It is used as a moisturizer, in hair products, in soaps and, in some regions, as a cooking fat.

Traditional use for dry skin and burns is well documented, and lab studies show anti-inflammatory compounds in it, but no trial found tests it alone for appearance.
quick.mechanism: It acts as an emollient, softening and coating the skin with fatty acids (mainly oleic and stearic). Lab work has examined triterpenes in the unsaponifiable fraction for anti-inflammatory activity.
quick.risks: Safety assessments cited by Grokipedia describe low toxicity for skin and oral use. Highly refined grades are reported to contain much less of the vitamin and phenolic content than raw butter.

lead: Shea butter is a fat extracted from the nuts of the shea tree (Vitellaria paradoxa), which grows wild across the dry savanna belt of West and Central Africa. It is mainly a triglyceride fat rich in oleic and stearic acids, ivory in colour when unrefined, and solid at room temperature but soft on the skin.[1][2]

For appearance, people use it as a rich emollient and skin conditioner: rubbed on dry or ashy skin to soften and add sheen, worked into hair and scalp for shine and slip, and found in moisturizers, lotions, lip balms, soaps and body butters.[1][16][17] Lifters on fitness forums mention it for moisturising after showers and for calming skin irritation.[16][17][22] Traditional use for dry skin, burns, rashes and wound care is documented in ethnomedical accounts from Sub-Saharan Africa.[2][11]

Research includes laboratory studies of its anti-inflammatory triterpene esters, controlled studies of shea-containing products such as a diaper emollient and a post-laser cream, and reviews that place it among plant butters and oils used on skin.[9][12][14][15] Few trials test shea butter alone for appearance outcomes.

angle.text: People rub shea butter on dry or ashy skin and into hair to soften it and add sheen. The fat is a rich emollient, and forum users describe using it after showers and on irritated areas.

paras: Shea butter is a fat from the kernel of the shea tree nut. The English name comes from the Bambara name for the tree, and the French karite is from Wolof.[1][18] The fat contains five principal fatty acids (palmitic, stearic, oleic, linoleic and arachidic), with stearic acid giving firmness and oleic acid softness. Wikipedia gives mean values of about 41.5 percent stearic and 46.4 percent oleic acid, and notes that composition varies by region: Ugandan butter is higher in oleic acid and liquid at warm temperatures, which is the source of liquid shea oil, while Burkina Faso butter tends to be harder.[1]

A 2014 review identified ten phenolic compounds in shea butter, eight of them catechins, with concentrations varying by region.[1] Grokipedia, an AI-generated source, reports that unsaponifiable matter such as triterpenes and sterols forms about 4 to 11 percent of the butter.[2] The unsaponifiable fraction is the part that laboratory work has examined for anti-inflammatory activity.[9]

Commercial butter is sold in three grades. Grade A is raw, unrefined and water-extracted, cream to greyish yellow with a nutty aroma; grade B is refined; grade C is highly refined, solvent-extracted with hexane, and pure white.[1][19] Wikipedia states that refining can remove up to 95 percent of the vitamin content while reducing contamination to undetectable levels.[1] Proponents of unrefined butter cite the retained vitamin and phenolic content, while refined grades are favoured in products where odour and colour matter.[1][2]

The raw butter is often coloured yellow by adding borututu root or palm oil.[1] Ethnomedical reviews note that traditional preparations were most often combined with other ingredients, most often African oil palm.[11]

The shea tree grows wild in the dry savannah belt of West and Central Africa, from Senegal east to Sudan and South Sudan and into the foothills of the Ethiopian highlands.[1][18] It is the only species in its genus and has two subspecies, with the older botanical name Butyrospermum parkii still common in the cosmetics trade.[18]

Archaeological evidence points to production at the medieval village of Saouga by the 14th century, and the butter was being imported into Britain by 1846.[1] Traditional production, carried out largely by women in rural communities, involves collecting fruits, removing the pulp, cracking and processing the kernels, roasting and pressing, then boiling, sieving and cooling the liquid.[2][18]

The tree is deciduous, typically 7 to 15 metres tall, begins bearing fruit at about 10 to 15 years and reaches full production at about 20 to 30, and can keep producing for up to 200 years. Fruits take four to six months to ripen and about 400 g of dry seed comes from each kilogram of fruit.[18]

In Africa the butter serves as food, medicine and cosmetic, and is described as a major dietary fat source. In Ghana and Nigeria it is a key ingredient in African black soap. In Lango and Acholi cultures of Uganda it is used in enthroning clan and traditional leaders, and practitioners of Afro-Brazilian religions in parts of Brazil use it in offerings.[18] The Ghanaian city of Tamale takes its name from a Dagbani phrase meaning home of shea nuts.[18]

A 2022 review of ethnomedicinal uses of shea butter for skin conditions in Sub-Saharan Africa identified 24 dermatologic uses across 30 references. Descriptive cross-sectional studies, often interviews and surveys, were the most common design; the most studied uses were scabies, wound healing and umbilical cord care; and the authors argued that wide traditional use justified more research.[11] A separate 2022 review of seven oils used for skin and scalp care in Nigeria reported that the oils contain fatty acids, triglycerides, ceramides, phospholipids, vitamins and antioxidants that may support barrier function and wound healing, and that adverse effects arose mainly from poor processing and storage hygiene.[13]

In cosmetics shea butter is used mainly as an emollient and skin conditioner in moisturizers, lotions, balms and soaps; people use it to soften dry skin and to add shine and slip to hair.[1] Product labels list it in items such as antiperspirant deodorant sprays.[5] It is also eaten in some African countries such as Benin and blended with other oils as a cocoa butter substitute, though the taste differs noticeably.[1]

DermNet New Zealand lists shea butter among anti-inflammatory ingredients added to moisturisers, alongside chamomile and aloe vera, within a framework in which emollients soften skin, occlusives such as petrolatum reduce water loss and humectants such as glycerine draw water into the outer layer.[20] Because shea butter is solid at room temperature and rich in stearic and oleic acid, it is used in body butters, soaps and hair products.[1]

DermNet lists burning or stinging in sensitive skin, allergic contact dermatitis to preservatives or fragrances in a vehicle, and aggravation of acne, folliculitis or perioral dermatitis by occlusive products among the recognised effects of moisturisers in general.[20]

sections.h: Use in fitness and looksmaxxing communities
paras: On T Nation, shea butter turns up mostly in everyday-care posts. One forum user wrote that baby oil sold with cocoa butter and shea butter, applied right after a shower, helped them avoid ashy skin; another described a shea and cocoa butter blend as not having a strong smell compared with regular baby oil.[16][17] A user joking about lotion on a physique photo asked whether the shine came from shea and cocoa butter.[21] A hiker reported using unscented shea butter to calm skin irritation, and a cook on the anabolic diet thread described frying pancakes in a little shea butter.[22][23]
The community discussion is mainly practical and anecdotal, concerning skin softness, ashiness, scent and texture, rather than the research literature.

A 2017 review of topical plant oils covered 19 oils and butters, shea butter among them, in terms of anti-inflammatory and antioxidant effects, wound healing and skin barrier repair.[3] A 2022 review of 27 clinical studies of 17 vegetable oils and butters, shea butter among them, concluded that on inflammation-affected skin oils high in oleic acid with little linoleic acid may further damage the stratum corneum, while oils high in linoleic acid and saturated fatty acids may be beneficial, and that frequency and duration of use matter; the abstract gives no shea-specific findings.[12]

In the laboratory, a 2010 study isolated eight triterpene esters (acetates and cinnamates of alpha-amyrin, beta-amyrin, lupeol and butyrospermol) from shea kernel fat. All showed marked anti-inflammatory activity in a mouse ear model, lupeol cinnamate was the most potent, and lupeol cinnamate also inhibited skin tumour promotion in a two-stage mouse model; the authors suggested shea fat may be a source of anti-inflammatory and anti-tumour-promoting compounds.[9] These are animal and cell studies, not studies of cosmetic use in people.

No clinical trial found tests shea butter on its own for appearance outcomes. Controlled studies have tested shea-containing products. A 1996 study of single applications of nine substances in 21 healthy volunteers, including shea butter and its unsaponifiable fraction, found no significant differences between substances on normal skin; on skin irritated with sodium lauryl sulphate, a sterol-enriched canola oil fraction reduced visible irritation and the other lipids tested did not affect irritation.[4]

A 2025 randomised crossover study in infants compared diapers with a shea butter-based emollient, a petrolatum-based emollient, or no emollient over six weeks. Babies in shea-emollient diapers were 2.6 times more likely to have a perianal erythema score of zero than in non-emollient diapers, with results similar to the petrolatum diaper, and adult forearm models showed similar protection.[14]

A split-face, double-blinded randomised trial of 20 subjects tested a moisturizing cream containing spent grain wax, argan kernel oil and shea butter extract, plus saccharide isomerate, against placebo after fractional CO2 laser; the active cream reduced erythema at day three and improved transepidermal water loss and skin capacitance by day seven, with no adverse events.[15] Registered studies have tested a related combination cream after a trichloroacetic acid peel (n=27) and in acne (n=20), and a soothing moisturizing lotion in atopic eczema.[6][7][8]
Studies of dietary fats high in stearic acid concern blood lipids and are not about skin.[10]

Grokipedia, an AI-generated source, states that safety assessments describe low toxicity for skin and oral use, and that adverse effects were generally not reported in cosmetic formulations.[2] Reviews of African oils attribute adverse effects mainly to poor processing and storage hygiene.[13] General moisturiser cautions from DermNet apply, including contact allergy to added ingredients and aggravation of acne by occlusive products.[20] Product labels for finished goods containing shea butter carry their own warnings; for example an antiperspirant spray lists flammability and use-on-broken-skin cautions.[5]

Traditional production is described as women's work in rural communities, and Grokipedia describes the butter as an income source for millions of women across the shea belt.[2] Wikipedia lists the shea tree as Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List and notes that Uganda's environmental authority has banned cutting shea trees.[18]

Grokipedia reports that in 2025 Nigeria introduced a six-month ban on raw shea nut exports to encourage local processing and that Ghana planned a phased ban by 2026; this is from an AI-generated source and is unverified.[2] A 2026 news report described a cooperative in Otuke District, Uganda, shipping 23 metric tonnes of processed shea butter to the United States, up from nine tonnes the year before, made from about 50 tonnes of nuts collected by about 1,000 rural women; its founder named poor infrastructure, limited affordable financing and high transport costs as constraints.[24] A second 2026 report in Uganda's Daily Monitor said high interest rates and market fragmentation were hurting exports.[25]

lore.intro: Shea butter appears in fitness and grooming forums as an everyday skin and hair moisturiser, mainly in short anecdotes about dry or ashy skin, irritation and texture.[16][17][22]

claims.claim: It keeps skin from looking ashy and dry
claims.believers: A T Nation user described applying shea and cocoa butter baby oil right after showering to keep skin looking fresh and clean.[16]
claims.experts: Emollients soften skin and occlusive ingredients reduce water loss, and DermNet lists shea butter among moisturiser ingredients; no trial found tests shea butter alone for dryness or ashiness.[20]

claims.claim: Unrefined shea butter is better than refined
claims.believers: Raw grade A butter keeps a nutty aroma and, per Wikipedia, more vitamin content than refined grades.[1][19]
claims.experts: Wikipedia states refining can remove up to 95 percent of vitamin content while reducing contaminants; no study found compares grades for appearance outcomes.[1]

claims.believers: A forum poster used unscented shea butter on irritation from ivy contact.[22]
claims.experts: Laboratory studies found anti-inflammatory activity of shea triterpene esters in mice, while a controlled human study found no effect of shea butter on irritation from sodium lauryl sulphate.[4][9]

claims.claim: Traditional uses on wounds, scabies and rashes show it heals skin
claims.believers: Ethnomedical surveys document use for scabies, wound healing and umbilical cord care, often combined with other ingredients.[11]
claims.experts: The review describes the evidence as largely descriptive surveys and calls for further research to assess potential.[11]

claims.believers: Grokipedia lists stretch marks among traditional dermatologic uses.[2]
claims.experts: A 2022 review of 27 clinical studies of vegetable butters and oils included striae among conditions studied, and no trial found tests shea butter alone for stretch marks.[12]

claims.claim: Oily butters are always good for inflamed skin
claims.believers: Plant oils and butters are widely used in moisturisers and described in reviews as supporting the barrier.[3]
claims.experts: A 2022 review concluded oleic-rich oils with little linoleic acid may further damage inflamed skin's stratum corneum, and DermNet notes occlusives can aggravate acne.[12][20]

claims.claim: It protects babies' skin as well as petrolatum
claims.believers: Manufacturers use shea butter-based emollients in diapers.[14]
claims.experts: A 2025 randomised crossover trial found the shea emollient diaper reduced erythema comparably to a petrolatum diaper.[14]
